extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, criminology, social history and political theory (graduate-level and above)
extracted.subtask_short: historical analysis of crime and state
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting historically situated, class-sensitive analyses of crime, criminalization, law and the state in capitalist societies; emphasizes relations between crime, political movements, ideological labelling, and modes of state hegemony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a more differentiated, historically located analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to reject simple common-sense accounts and to provide a more differentiated, historically located analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by drawing fine-grained historical distinctions rather than assuming 'that is that'. Analysis must unravel the historical 'logic' and rationale of events (e.g. mugging) rather than treating them as self-evident facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish deviant crimes from crimes expressing social protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw distinctions between crimes which are 'deviant' with respect to their means but consonant with societal norms, and crimes which express an element of social protest or opposition to the existing order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this distinction provisionally and cautiously; identify social/political content where present and avoid collapsing all criminality into a single category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare scale of criminal activity with scale of containment
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate occasions where the scale of criminal activity and measures to contain it are in rough balance (normalised repression) from occasions where there's a radical discrepancy between 'threat' and 'containment'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify 'moments' where containment escalates rapidly or crime patterns change, as these often coincide with wider historical crises and require special analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify 'moments of more than usual alarm' and their historical significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Moments of 'more than usual alarm' followed by 'more than normal control' have tended to coincide with periods of profound social upheaval, economic crisis and historical rupture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat spikes in alarm/control as potential indicators of larger political/historical conjunctures rather than isolated policing responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'ordinary' crime and 'social' crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the distinction between 'ordinary' crime and 'social' crime—types of criminal activity that express a conscious, almost political challenge to the prevailing order (Hobsbawm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that while differences are important, they are difficult to sustain definitively; use the distinction as an analytic tool rather than a rigid taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating 'crime' as fixed natural categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal and social crime are not fixed statuses or 'natural' categories; assignment to categories and use of the 'criminal' tag is often part of broader strategies of repression and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'crime' as a provisional category through which to construct more complex, historically grounded accounts; avoid the historical error of reifying criminal subcultures as isolated entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate criminal subcultures to wider class ecologies and 'working-class repertoire'
rubrics_metrics.description: Study criminal fraternities and subcultures as parts of wider class ecologies, cultural repertoires and stratified class formations rather than as separate, isolated phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruct criminal behaviour in relation to work-poverty-unemployment dynamics and the broader repertoire of working-class responses; use examples (e.g. East London) to show embeddedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historicize changing definitions of crime and the role of criminalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime is differently defined at different periods; changing definitions reflect shifting applications of the category by governing classes often to prepare the ground for legal restraint and political control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how the attachment of the criminal label legitimizes judicial control and how ideological work shifts labels (e.g. deserving/undeserving) until they stick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine convergence and movement between political and criminal activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse both convergences from political into criminal strategies (e.g. Bonnot Gang, Angry Brigade) and from criminal into political (e.g. Malcolm X, politicisation in prison movements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming pure separations; investigate cases where political movements adopt criminal strategies and where criminals become politicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat law as instrument of class authority and educator of property norms
rubrics_metrics.description: The law functions as an instrument of class domination and as a public 'educator' of property and respect for property (e.g. Black Act, Blackstone, Hay, Thompson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse legislation, courtroom ritual, public executions and judicial practice as ways the law shapes ideology and social consent as well as repression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for changing role and 'autonomisation' of the law across historical periods
rubrics_metrics.description: The law becomes, gradually and unevenly, less arbitrary, more 'impartial', more 'autonomous' (rule of law, separation of powers), altering its relation to class power and the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both gains (real justice for the poor, protections) and continuities (defence of private property, public-order functions) when historicizing the law's evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge the myth of judicial neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: The political neutrality of the judiciary is a myth; judicial decisions often embody political, moral and social prejudices framed as 'public interest'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize claims of impartiality and consider how judicial rhetoric masks class-aligned interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use but critique the 'societal control culture' concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemert's 'societal control culture'—the laws, procedures, programs and organizations that in the name of the collectivity manipulate deviants—helps highlight links between agencies and shared ideological perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize its utility in showing institutional/ideological linkages, but avoid over-reliance: it lacks historical specificity and doesn't provide a theory of the state or differentiate types of regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return analysis of law to a theory of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Law, crime, social control, legality/illegality, conformity and opposition must be posed in relation to the capitalist state and the class struggle; the law is centrally connected with modes of hegemony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate empirical studies (e.g. 'mugging') within a broader, historically specific state-theoretical framework (post-laissez-faire/Welfare State, crisis in hegemony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate repressive and consensual functions of state apparatuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine both the repressive and the consensual/legitimating functions of juridical and state apparatuses and how they interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat state institutions as monolithic; analyse how coercion and consent are produced and balanced across time and regime types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject ahistorical 'control-culture' accounts; specify state type and historical conjuncture
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'control-culture' approach is too imprecise because it does not locate centres of power historically, differentiate types of state/regime, or examine repressive vs consensual functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the specific social formation and political regime (e.g. parliamentary democracy, welfare-state) when explaining crime-control configurations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a materially grounded Marxist theory of law, crime and the state (without reductionism)
rubrics_metrics.description: While Marxist elements exist, there is no fully elaborated theory in Marx/Engels; it is necessary to work out a more developed, non-reductive materialist theory linking law, crime and state to material conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid simplistic formulae (e.g. law merely reflects bourgeois economic relations); instead state more fully the concepts of law, crime and state on which analysis is based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse the hierarchy of credibility and power to label
rubrics_metrics.description: If labelling is central to identification and control of deviance, then the question of who has the power to label whom (Becker's 'hierarchy of credibility') is of critical importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace institutional authority and ideological resources that allow some actors (police, media, judiciary) to impose labels with greater social effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study processes and routes into/out of crime rather than static categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on processes rather than categories: the routes individuals take into and out of crime are variable and historically contingent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reconstruction of life-histories and contextual drivers over assigning people permanently to 'criminal' statuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine ideological work in shifting labels and legitimating control
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the ideological transformations and label-shifting work (e.g. deserving/undeserving, labouring/dangerous) that legitimate legal restraint and social control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse media, political rhetoric and legal language as active ingredients in widening labels' reference and winning social support for 'tough measures'.
